    AI Overview
    View all
    Hydrocodone is a powerful, addictive opioid analgesic used to treat severe, chronic pain or severe cough. It works by binding to CNS opioid receptors to change the body’s perception of pain. Common side effects include nausea, dizziness, constipation, and drowsiness, and it can cause fatal respiratory depression or dependency. 
    Common Brand Names (Combined or Extended-Release)
     
    • Combination (e.g., with Acetaminophen): Vicodin®, Lortab®, Lorcet-HD
    • Extended-Release (ER): Hysingla® ER, Zohydro® ER 
    Key Information 
    • Usage: Prescribed for moderate to severe pain when other treatments are insufficient, or for cough suppression.
    • Side Effects: Common side effects include constipation, dizziness, drowsiness, headache, nausea, and vomiting. Serious effects include severe respiratory depression, liver injury (if combined with acetaminophen), and hypotension.
    • Mechanism: As a CNS depressant, it works as an antitussive (cough suppressor) and reduces pain sensation in the brain.
    • Withdrawal Symptoms: Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal, including anxiety, insomnia, nausea, tremors, and vomiting.
    • Warnings: It is a high-risk medication that can cause addiction and dependence. Do not mix with alcohol or drive until you know how it affects you. 
    Physical Appearance
    Hydrocodone pills are often oval-shaped, typically orange, white, or yellow, and labeled with their milligram dosage.

    Is hydrocodone a strong pill?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Yes, hydrocodone is a strong, highly addictive opioid medication
     used for severe pain, with a potency similar to morphine. It acts as a central nervous system depressant and is often combined with non-opioid pain relievers like acetaminophen, bringing risks of addiction, abuse, and life-threatening breathing issues. 
    Key facts about hydrocodone: 
    • Purpose: Treats moderate to severe pain and sometimes used as a cough suppressant.
    • Strength: Considered a potent opioid, though often slightly less potent than oxycodone.
    • Addiction Risk: High risk of addiction, dependency, and abuse.
    • Side Effects: Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, and drowsiness.
    • Overdose Danger: Can cause fatal respiratory depression (stopped breathing), especially when combined with alcohol. 
    Hydrocodone is generally intended for short-term use under strict medical supervision.

      AI Overview
      Hydrocodone is an opioid analgesic that treats moderate-to-severe pain by binding to mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system, specifically in the brain and spinal cord. It inhibits pain signal transmission, reduces pain perception, and triggers dopamine release, while often paired with acetaminophen for enhanced efficacy. 
      Key Mechanisms of Action:
      • Pain Relief:
        As a mu-opioid agonist, it alters the brain's response to pain, inhibiting the release of neurotransmitters. 
      • Onset and Duration:
        It typically takes effect within 10 to 20 minutes and lasts for 4-6 hours (immediate-release), while extended-release versions can last 12-24 hours. 
      • Central Nervous System Effect:
        It suppresses coughs and can cause dizziness or drowsiness by affecting the nervous system. 
      Important Safety Information:
      • Risks: It carries a high risk of addiction, physical dependence, and potentially fatal respiratory depression (slowed breathing). 
      • Side Effects: Common side effects include constipation, nausea, dizziness, and sedation. 
      • Withdrawal: Sudden cessation can lead to withdrawal, so gradual reduction is usually necessary. 
      It is frequently combined with non-opioid pain relievers like acetaminophen (e.g., Norco, Vicodin) to improve pain control, but this poses a risk of liver toxicity if overused.

        AI Overview
        Hydrocodone is an opioid medication with common side effects including drowsiness, dizziness, constipation, nausea, vomiting, and lightheadedness. Serious risks include respiratory depression (slowed breathing), addiction, severe hypotension, and potential liver damage if combined with acetaminophen. It requires careful medical supervision. 
        Common Side Effects: 
        • Constipation: A very common, often persistent side effect.
        • Central Nervous System Depressants: Drowsiness, dizziness, lightheadedness, and sedation.
        • Gastrointestinal Distress: Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
        • Others: Headache, dry mouth, and sweating.
        Serious Side Effects (Seek Immediate Medical Care):
        • Respiratory Issues: Slow, shallow, or shallow breathing; noisy breathing; or sleep apnea. 
        • Allergic Reactions: Hives, itching, rash, or swelling of the face, tongue, or throat. 
        • Mental Changes: Confusion, severe agitation, or hallucinations. 
        • Other Potential Issues: Seizures, severe dizziness/fainting, or symptoms of low blood sugar. 
        Warnings & Long-Term Effects:
        • Addiction and Dependence:
          Long-term use can lead to physical dependence, tolerance, and addiction. 
        • Withdrawal Symptoms:
          Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal, including restlessness, muscle pain, insomnia, diarrhea, and vomiting. 
        • Overdose:
          Symptoms include extreme sleepiness, pinpoint pupils, cold/clammy skin, and coma. 
        • Interaction:
          Do not consume alcohol or other sedating drugs, as this increases the risk of fatal respiratory depression. 
        Disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only. Always consult a healthcare provider for medical advice.

          An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
          AI Overview
          Hydrocodone pills exist primarily as combination products with acetaminophen or ibuprofen, available in immediate-release (IR) tablets and capsules (e.g., Vicodin, Norco) or extended-release (ER) formulations (e.g., Zohydro ER). Common IR dosage strengths range from 2.5mg to 10mg, while ER formulations can range up to 120mg. 
          • Common Combination Tablets (IR):
            • Hydrocodone/Acetaminophen (APAP): Commonly found as Vicodin, Norco, Lortab, and generic forms. Strengths usually include 5mg, 7.5mg, or 10mg of hydrocodone combined with 300mg or 325mg of acetaminophen. 
            • Hydrocodone/Ibuprofen: Examples include Vicoprofen and Reprexain, usually containing 7.5mg hydrocodone and 200mg ibuprofen. 
          • Extended-Release (ER) Capsules/Tablets:
            • Zohydro ER: Extended-release capsules containing only hydrocodone bitartrate, designed to release medication over 12 hours. Common strengths are 10mg, 15mg, 20mg, 30mg, 40mg, and 50mg. 
            • Hysingla ER: A 24-hour abuse-deterrent, extended-release tablet. 
          • Physical Appearance:
            • IR combination tablets are typically white, yellow, or pink, and may be oval, round, or oblong in shape, often imprinted with numbers or manufacturer details. 
            • ER capsules are generally larger, with specific markings indicating their extended-release formulation. 
          • Note on Dosage:
            Due to the risk of abuse and liver toxicity (from APAP), these are tightly regulated and prescribed based on pain level, with immediate-release versions generally taken every 4–6 hours.

            AI Overview
            Hydrocodone, a semi-synthetic opioid derived from codeine, was first synthesized in Germany in 1920 by Carl Mannich and Helene Löwenheim. Initially used for cough suppression, it was FDA-approved in 1943 (as Hycodan) and gained popularity in the 1950s for pain management, later becoming widely known in combinations like Vicodin (1983) and Norco. It is now a Schedule II controlled substance used for severe pain, with misuse leading to stricter regulations in the 2010s. 
            Key Historical Milestones & Usage Examples
            • 1920: Synthesized in Germany from thebaine, a component of opium. 
            • 1923: First report suggesting potential for euphoria and habituation. 
            • 1943: FDA approved the first hydrocodone product (Hycodan) for cough suppression. 
            • 1950s: Widespread use and adoption of hydrocodone products in the US. 
            • 1961: First report on physical dependence and addiction. 
            • 1983: FDA approval of Vicodin, a combination of hydrocodone and acetaminophen, which popularized the drug for pain relief. 
            • 2014: The DEA tightened regulations, moving all hydrocodone products from Schedule III to Schedule II due to high abuse potential. 
            Synonyms and Common Brand Names
            Hydrocodone is a semisynthetic mu-opiate receptor agonist, and its formulations often contain other analgesics. 
            • Common Brand Names: Vicodin, Norco, Lortab, Hycodan, Vicoprofen, Lorcet-HD.
            • Common Street Names/Aliases: Vike, Watson.
            Evolution of Medical Usage
            Historically, it was commonly used for cough suppression, but modern usage is overwhelmingly focused on treating moderate-to-moderately severe pain, often in combination with acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Due to the opioid crisis, prescriptions have declined from over 68 million in 2014 to around 30 million in the early 2020s.

              AI Overview
              Hydrocodone, commonly combined with acetaminophen in pills (e.g., Norco, Vicodin), has the chemical formula
              C18H21NO3cap C sub 18 cap H sub 21 cap N cap O sub 3
              and IUPAC name 4,5α-epoxy-3-methoxy-17-methylmorphinan-6-one.                             It is a semi-synthetic opioid related to codeine, appearing as fine, white crystals in its bitartrate form, often structured in tablet or capsule forms. 
              Chemical Structure Details
              • Formula:
                C18H21NO3cap C sub 18 cap H sub 21 cap N cap O sub 3
                (Hydrocodone base) or
                C18H21NO3⋅C4H6O6⋅212H2Ocap C sub 18 cap H sub 21 cap N cap O sub 3 center dot cap C sub 4 cap H sub 6 cap O sub 6 center dot 2 and one-half cap H sub 2 cap O
                (Hydrocodone bitartrate hydrate).                 
              • Structure Components: A methoxy group, a methyl group, and a 6-one carbonyl group within a morphinan skeleton. 
              • Synonyms: Dihydrocodeinone, 4,5-epoxy-3-methoxy-N-methyl-6-oxomorphinane, Hydrocone, and Dicodid. 
              • Appearance: Fine, white crystals or crystalline powder. 
              Usage Examples and Context
              • Analgesic: Used primarily for moderate to severe pain relief. 
              • Antitussive: Used to treat severe coughs. 
              • Common Formulations: Combined with Acetaminophen (5 mg/325 mg, 7.5 mg/325 mg, 10 mg/325 mg) in branded products like Norco, Vicodin, and Lortab. 
              • Inactive Ingredients: Often includes croscarmellose sodium, magnesium stearate, and microcrystalline cellulose. 
              Hydrocodone acts as a full opioid agonist at the
              μmu
              -              opioid receptor, affecting the central nervous system to reduce pain, and is classified as a controlled substance due to its high potential for addiction and abuse.
